title: Duplication Over Coupling
gist: Domain partitioning taken to its physical limit: one bounded context per service, its own database inside it, and duplication preferred to reuse. The style that earns the most five-star ratings in the book, and charges for every one.
minute: Built on **bounded context**. Everything a subdomain needs lives inside the service — code, schema, database. Nothing couples across the boundary, which is why it is called a *share nothing* architecture.
**Reuse is implemented via coupling**, so this style deliberately chooses **duplication over reuse**. A shared `Address` class is a coupling point, and it gets copied instead.
The one thing it *does* share is operational: the **Sidecar** pattern plus a **service mesh** gives every service the same monitoring, logging and circuit breakers without domain coupling.

**“Micro” is a label, not a description.** Too-fine services (the *Grains of Sand* antipattern) force communication back in and produce a big ball of distributed mud. Find boundaries by purpose, transactions and choreography cost.
**Database-per-service** is not optional here — a shared database breaks the bounded context outright. And the advice on distributed transactions is blunt: **don't. Fix the granularity instead.**

sections.t: Topology: a service is a bounded context
sections.alt: An API layer above five services, each inside a dashed bounded context with its own database
sections.cap: Fig. 18-1 · each service runs in its own process, in a VM or container, with everything it needs inside.
sections.p: Named unusually early — Martin Fowler and James Lewis's 2014 post defined it rather than describing something already common. It is heavily inspired by domain-driven design, and it **physically embodies** DDD's logical bounded context.
items: **The API layer** (usually a gateway) sits between consumers and services and handles **routing and cross-cutting concerns only** — security, monitoring, logging, naming. Putting orchestration or business logic in it violates the philosophy: mediators belong to technically partitioned architectures, and this one is firmly domain partitioned.

**Frontends**: the original vision put the UI inside the bounded context. Web partitioning makes that hard, so in practice you see either a **monolithic frontend** calling through the API layer, or **micro-frontends** — UI components matched one-to-one with backend services.
**Performance is the standing cost.** Network calls dwarf method calls, and a security check at every endpoint adds more. Which puts granularity at the centre of everything.

sections.t: Granularity, and how to find it
sections.alt: A choreographed front-controller service beside an orchestrated mediator
sections.cap: Three questions for where the boundary goes.
items: **Purpose** — each service should be functionally cohesive, contributing one significant behaviour to the application. The domain is the first source of boundaries.
**Transactions** — entities that must cooperate in a transaction suggest a boundary. Designing to *avoid* distributed transactions tends to produce better designs anyway.
**Choreography** — a set of services with beautiful domain isolation that has to talk constantly is a candidate for being bundled back into one coarser service.
quotes: The term microservice is a label, not a description.
It was named to contrast with the dominant style of 2007, service-oriented architecture — which could equally have been called “gigantic services”. Many developers read the prefix as a commandment.
sections.p: **Iteration is the only way to get this right.** Nobody discovers the right granularity, data dependencies and communication style on the first pass.

sections.t: The one thing it shares: operations
sections.alt: Five services each with a sidecar, all wired into a service plane forming a mesh
sections.cap: Figs. 18-2 to 18-4 · domain concerns duplicated, operational concerns shared deliberately.
sections.p: Traditional SOA reused everything, domain and operational alike. Microservices splits them: circuit breaker, logging and monitoring live in a **sidecar** owned by a shared infrastructure team, and the sidecars wire into a **service plane** (Istio and similar) to form a **service mesh**. Upgrading the monitoring tool is then one team's change rather than forty teams' backlog items — and **service discovery** usually rides in the same place, giving elasticity somewhere consistent to live.
items: **Protocol-aware heterogeneous interoperability** is the communication model. *Protocol-aware*: with no integration hub, each service must know or discover how to call the others. *Heterogeneous*: full polyglot support, since each service can be a different stack. *Interoperability*: services do call each other over the network.

One architect took this to its logical end: **mandating that every team use a different technology stack**, so that sharing a class accidentally became impossible. The opposite of most enterprise standardisation, and the point stands — not every service needs an industrial-strength relational database.

sections.alt: A choreographed front-controller service beside an orchestrated mediator
sections.sit: A business process spans six services. There is no global mediator in this style — so either the services call each other as needed, or you build a service whose only job is coordination.
opts: Choreography — services call each other directly.

Preserves the decoupling that the whole style exists for, and performs better: less coupling, faster communication, fewer bottlenecks. For a simple case — wish list calling demographics for a missing field — it is obviously right.
Orchestration — build a local mediator service.
Coupling concentrates in one place and the other services stay simple. You have created coupling deliberately, in a spot you chose.
sections.verdict: Neither is right; watch for the failure mode. In a complex workflow, choreography quietly produces the **Front Controller pattern** — the first service called becomes a mediator *in addition to* its own domain responsibilities, and carries both complexities. **Domain workflows are often inherently coupled**; the architect's job is choosing where to represent that coupling, not pretending it isn't there.

sections.alt: A mediator coordinating four services where one fails and the successful ones must be undone
sections.sit: Two services need to update together atomically. In a monolith this was one commit. Here they are separate services with separate databases.
opts: Wire a distributed transaction across them.
This violates the core decoupling principle *and* creates **Connascence of Values** across services — the worst dynamic form in the vocabulary from Chapter 3.
Fix the granularity: put them in one service.
The book's actual advice, stated plainly. Needing transactions to hold your microservices together is a sign the design is **too granular**.
Use a Saga, if the boundaries genuinely must differ.

The legitimate exception — two services needing genuinely different architecture characteristics. A mediator calls each part, records success or failure, and on failure sends **compensating transactions** to undo the parts that succeeded, usually with requests held pending until overall success.
sections.verdict: Compensating transactions generate substantial network coordination traffic, and juggling asynchronous requests gets hard fast when new requests depend on pending transactional state. The line worth remembering: **a few transactions crossing services is sometimes necessary; if it is the dominant feature of the architecture, microservices is the wrong choice.** *Software Architecture: The Hard Parts* catalogues eight Saga patterns for the cases where you do need one.

sections.t: Two services need the same table
sections.alt: Sixty services on one database, database-per-service, and a wider bounded context of three services sharing one database
sections.sit: You have split payment processing into credit card, gift card, PayPal and rewards points. All four write to and read the same data. Database-per-service says four databases.
opts: With sixty services sharing a database, renaming a column means coordinating sixty deployments with a schema release. Worse, the bounded context has stopped existing — and databases rarely scale with the service instances around them.
Correct by the rule and wrong for this case: they genuinely need the same data, so you have created four services that must synchronise constantly.
Let those services share a database, inside a wider bounded context.

A bounded context does not have to contain exactly one service. Draw it around the payment types — or the shipping methods — and let them share. **No more than five or six**, or the change-control, scalability and fault-tolerance problems return.
sections.verdict: **Database-per-service is the standard topology here and the one that preserves the bounded context**: other services request data through a contract, so they are decoupled from the internal structure, and you can swap a relational database for a document database without telling anyone. The trade-off of a wider context is exactly the one you re-accept: a schema change now coordinates several deployments.

sections.t: Characteristics, risks, and when to reach for it

gen.head: MICROSERVICES — DOMAIN PARTITIONED · MANY QUANTA
rows: some of the most scalable systems built
one vital sign fails, the rest monitor on
scope of a change is one service
network calls, security checks, data latency

sections.cap: Fig. 18-16 · the most distinct quanta of any modern architecture. In many ways it is what the quantum measure was invented to describe.
items: **Grains of Sand** — services made too fine because *micro* was read as a size instruction. The fix is combining them into coarser services.
**Too much interservice communication** — usually the same root cause, and the same fix.
**Too much data sharing** — costs exactly the change control, scalability, fault tolerance and agility that this style is chosen for.

**Shared code.** Reuse through a common JAR or DLL spreads one bounded context across several, so a change to shared code can break services elsewhere. Versioning helps and does not remove the complication.

**Governance**: watch static coupling (shared libraries, contracts) with a software bill of materials and dependency tooling; watch dynamic coupling by having every service log its outbound calls consistently, or by having services register their interservice calls to a configuration server like ZooKeeper, then querying it for a map of the whole ecosystem.
sections.p: On **serverless**: the authors do not treat it as an architecture style but as a **deployment model of microservices** — a single-purpose, separately deployed unit that does one thing is the definition of both. Microservices deploys equally well as containers under Kubernetes. The worked example is a patient vital-signs monitor: one service per vital sign, each with its own store, sharing only *Alert Staff* and *Display Vital Signs* — and if the blood-pressure service crashes, every other vital sign keeps being watched.

source: Fundamentals of Software Architecture: An Engineering Approach, 2nd ed. — Mark Richards & Neal Ford (O'Reilly, 2025). Chapter 18: Microservices Architecture, pp. 329–357.
